title: the life of a process is asked in one place, and a zombie is dead
intent: The wave moves the reader of the tree of the processes from the support of the checks into the kernel and gives the kernel the RULE of the life of a process.  (1) **One reader, in the kernel.**  The module `tests/support/yeah-proc.el` (92 lines, 4 143 bytes) becomes `lib/yeah-proc.el` (127 lines, 5 961 bytes): the reading of the state and of the ticks of a process lives in the kernel now, and the support of the checks is gone.  (2) **The rule of the life lives in one place.**  The new function `yeah-proc-alive-p` answers the question whether a process lives by its STATE: `S' and `R' live, `Z' is a zombie -- a process that is dead and waits to be reaped --, and every other letter is a process that does not run; the state nil is the state of a process that is not there at all, and such a process does not live.  The question whether a process lives has its answer in the state of the process, and the tree of the processes cannot answer it: the directory of a zombie is there as well, and a caller that asks for that directory calls a zombie alive.  (3) **The kernel asks the rule.**  `lib/yeah-life.el` loses its own `yeah-life--owner-alive-p`; both of its call sites ask `(yeah-proc-alive-p (yeah-proc-state pid))` now.  Two consequences follow, and they are the point of the wave: the socket of a ZOMBIE owner is swept away (a socket of a zombie must not keep a service from starting), and `yeah-life-adopt` does not refuse a zombie owner as if it lived.  (4) **The checks ask the rule.**  Six checks of `tests/checks/` that read 'the process is alive' by the existence of the directory of the process -- a zombie answers that too -- read the state of the process now: `check-a-pilot-that-is-interrupted-leaves-no-server.el`, `check-a-check-that-is-killed-leaves-no-server.el`, `check-a-check-that-hangs-is-stopped.el`, `check-a-killed-gate-run-restarts-and-reaches-the-end.el`, `check-a-server-left-behind-is-gone.el`, `check-a-killed-run-leaves-no-copy-behind.el` (which loses a rule that was never called at all).  The three checks of the waves 100 and 101 read the process through the module of the kernel as well.  (5) **The picture names the module.**  `site/diagrams/core-layers.puml` names `lib/yeah-proc.el:69` in the block of the execution scheduler -- next to `lib/yeah-life.el`, the module that asks the rule; the completeness of the picture is part of its promise.  (6) **The proof of the wave.**  The new check `tests/checks/check-a-process-that-is-dead-is-dead-everywhere.el` (296 lines, 14 035 bytes) holds four parts: the rule answers by the letter of the state; a STAND compares the new rule with the old one on one subject (the old rule -- `file-directory-p` on the directory of the process -- says 'alive' for a zombie, the new rule says 'dead', and for a living process both say 'alive', so the live is not broken); the rule is not smeared (no other file of the repository defines a rule of the life of a process, and a file that asks the rule asks the state as well); and the readings of the kernel still decide (the state of a living process is one letter).  The zombie of the stand is the letter `Z', not a living zombie: a child that ends at once is reaped before the window of the check opens, and a proof that depends on that race is a proof that cannot fail.  (7) **The naming follows the convention.**  `ELISP_BEST_PRACTICES.md` §2 (Naming) says that a symbol which could be called from another module uses a single dash.  The reader of the kernel is called from `lib/yeah-life.el` and from the checks, so `yeah-proc--state', `yeah-proc--ticks' and `yeah-proc--alive-p' are renamed to `yeah-proc-state', `yeah-proc-ticks' and `yeah-proc-alive-p'; `yeah-proc--stat-text' and `yeah-proc--number' stay internal.  (8) **The claim of the wave is new**: `a-process-that-is-dead-is-dead-everywhere`.  The claim of the wave 100 keeps its id, its falsifier, its requirements and its kind; its TEXT names the new place of the reader, its SCOPE names the new file, and its CONTROL follows the file that moved -- the amendment of a claim follows the code that moved, and the wave says so.
objection: The wave moves a rule into the kernel, and the price is named.  (a) **The wave does not weaken the checks it moved.**  The six checks that read the life of a process still fail when the process lives and passes when it does not; the change is in the question they ask, not in what they prove.  The old question -- 'does the directory of the process exist?' -- is true of a zombie, so it could pass a check whose subject was dead; the new question is the state of the process, and the check of the wave proves that the new question and the old one differ on a zombie and agree on a living process.  (b) **The wave does not invent a zombie.**  The proof of the wave is a stand on the letter of the state: a real zombie cannot be made to appear on demand (a child that ends at once is reaped before the window of the check opens), and a proof that waits for a race is a proof that cannot fail.  What is proven is the RULE, and the rule is what the checks ask.  (c) **The wave does not close the class of the defect.**  The survey of 2026-11-21 found 42 places of the class and named 19 dangerous; this wave closes seven of them (six checks and the kernel rule).  `scripts/lib/tree.sh:46-50' (the awk over the glob of the stat files dies on a file that vanishes and cuts the list of the descendants short) and `lib/yeah-client.el:62-64' (the file of the port is deleted by the stop of the service and the client falls where its docstring promises nil) are the waves 102 and 103.  (d) **The amendment of the claim of the wave 100 is an amendment and not a rewrite.**  Its id, its falsifier, its requirements and its kind are the same; the text names the new place of the reader, the scope names the new file, and the control follows the file that moved.  The scope of two other claims grows by the same file for the same reason: `the-server-does-not-spin-when-the-provider-is-silent' and `the-pilot-that-runs-out-of-time-leaves-no-server-behind' read the process through the reader, and the reader lives in the kernel now.  (e) **The wave changes the behaviour of the kernel in one place, and the change is named.**  The socket of a zombie owner is swept and `yeah-life-adopt` no longer refuses a zombie owner; before the wave, a service whose owner was a zombie kept a socket that nobody could take, and the service could not start.  (f) **The rename is a decision of the parent, and it is recorded as such.**  The prescription of the wave named `yeah-proc--state' and the like; `ELISP_BEST_PRACTICES.md` §2 (Naming) requires a single dash for a symbol called from another module.  The writer of the wave reported the contradiction instead of resolving it silently, and the parent resolved it on 2026-11-21: the convention of the project wins over the wording of the prescription.
refuted_by: the rule of the life of a process calls a zombie alive, or the state of a process that is gone is not nil, or the state of a process that lives is not one letter, or a check of tests/checks/ asks whether the directory of a process exists instead of asking its state, or a file of lib/ reads the stat file of a process by itself, or the socket of a zombie owner is not swept, or the control of the claim does not make the check fail by its own assertion
note: The wave is the answer to the survey, not to the gate.  (1) **The survey (read-only, 2026-11-21)** counted 42 places of the class 'the reader falls on the filesystem where it promised nil' and named 19 of them dangerous (9 high, 10 medium).  Three of them matter: the six checks that read 'alive' by the existence of the directory of the process (a zombie answers that too), the awk of `scripts/lib/tree.sh:46-50' and the port file of `lib/yeah-client.el:62-64'.  (2) **This wave closes the first of the three**, and it closes it in the kernel rather than in the checks: a check that asks the rule of the kernel cannot drift from it.  (3) **The measure of the wave**: `lib/yeah-proc.el` -- 127 lines and 5 961 bytes; the new check -- 296 lines and 14 035 bytes; six checks of `tests/checks/` moved to the rule of the kernel; three checks of the waves 100 and 101 read the process through the module of the kernel; the support `tests/support/yeah-proc.el' is gone.  (4) **The naming**: `ELISP_BEST_PRACTICES.md` §2 (Naming) -- 'anything that could be called from another module uses a single dash'; the three functions that the kernel and the checks call were renamed (commit `8a22cf3'), the two that only the module calls were not.  The writer of the wave reported the contradiction between the prescription and the convention, and the parent decided on 2026-11-21 (a decision outside §17.2; the owner may cancel it).  (5) **The finding F39 (the projection of the interface writes the answer `allow-always' as a refusal) is outside this wave** and waits for C1: both touch the same record of a decision of a permission.
